meta.sourceLabel: Curated real black hole parameters, one citation per field
notes: Spec §6.4: every parameter carries its own citation string and an uncertainty flag. Where a quantity is poorly constrained the UI says so rather than picking a number that looks confident.

uncertainty is one of: measured (a published value with a real error bar), contested (published values disagree beyond their stated errors), unconstrained (no measurement worth quoting; the value is a plausible placeholder chosen so the renderer has something to draw).
spin is the dimensionless Kerr parameter a* = Jc/GM^2, always in [0, 1) here — every object listed is prograde or unconstrained, so no negative (retrograde) values appear.

inclinationDeg is the viewing angle of the accretion flow: 0 is face-on (looking down the spin axis), 90 is edge-on. For the X-ray binaries this is the orbital inclination, which is not necessarily the inner-disk inclination; for M87* it is the jet axis angle. That distinction is stated per object in the inclination source string.
raDeg/decDeg are J2000 in degrees and exist for milestone 11 (sky dots on the globe), not for the simulator. Positions are direction-only: nothing is ever placed at a true distance.
distanceKpc is kiloparsecs. Multiply by 3261.564 for light-years.

objects.name: Sagittarius A*
objects.blurb: The Milky Way's own black hole, 26,000 light-years away behind the galactic centre. Big enough that the tides at the horizon would not tear a person apart.

solarMasses.source: GRAVITY Collaboration (2022), 'Mass distribution in the Galactic Center based on interferometric astrometry of multiple stellar orbits' — 4.297e6 M☉ with R0 = 8277 pc

spin.source: EHT Collaboration (2022), Sgr A* Paper V — the data prefer non-zero prograde spin but do not pin a value; 0.5 is a placeholder, not a measurement

inclinationDeg.source: EHT Collaboration (2022), Sgr A* Paper V — models with inclination ≤ 50° are preferred and low-inclination MAD models perform best; 30° sits inside that band

jets.source: No prominent large-scale jet is observed from Sgr A*; it is a strikingly under-luminous accretor

objects.name: Cygnus X-1
objects.blurb: The first object widely accepted as a black hole, and the subject of a famous Hawking–Thorne bet. It is fed by the wind of a blue supergiant companion.

solarMasses.source: Miller-Jones et al. (2021), Science 371, 1046 — 21.2 ± 2.2 M☉, revised upward with the new parallax distance

spin.source: Zhao et al. (2021), 'Re-estimating the Spin Parameter of the Black Hole in Cygnus X-1' — a* > 0.9985 (3σ) by continuum fitting with the revised mass and distance

inclinationDeg.source: Miller-Jones et al. (2021) — orbital inclination 27.5 ± 0.8°, close to face-on

distanceKpc.source: Miller-Jones et al. (2021) — 2.22 (+0.18/−0.17) kpc by radio parallax (VLBA)

jets.source: A compact, resolved radio jet is seen in the hard state; it is not a superluminal ejector like GRS 1915+105

objects.name: GRS 1915+105
objects.blurb: The archetypal microquasar: a stellar-mass black hole that fires superluminal radio ejections, the reason the word 'microquasar' exists at all.

solarMasses.source: Reid et al. (2014), ApJ 796, 2 — 12.4 (+2.0/−1.8) M☉, revised down from earlier ~14 M☉ estimates by the parallax distance

spin.source: Reflection fits give a* = 0.98 ± 0.01 while continuum fitting with the Reid distance gives substantially lower values — the methods disagree beyond their quoted errors

inclinationDeg.source: Reid et al. (2014) give 60 ± 5° for the binary; X-ray reflection fits prefer ~71°, so the inner disk may be misaligned with the orbit

distanceKpc.source: Reid et al. (2014) — 8.6 (+2.0/−1.6) kpc by trigonometric parallax (VLBA)

jets.source: Mirabel & Rodríguez (1994) reported apparently superluminal ejections; the source has fired repeated relativistic jets since

objects.name: V404 Cygni
objects.blurb: A transient that spends decades quiet and then erupts — its 2015 outburst was bright enough to be followed by amateur telescopes.

solarMasses.source: Khargharia et al. (2010) — 9.0 (+0.2/−0.6) M☉ from near-infrared spectroscopy of the K3 III donor

spin.source: No agreed spin measurement; published constraints span most of the allowed range. 0.5 is a placeholder, not a measurement

inclinationDeg.source: Khargharia et al. (2010), consistent with Casares & Charles (1994) and Shahbaz et al. (1994) — 67°, well toward edge-on

distanceKpc.source: Miller-Jones et al. (2009) — 2.39 ± 0.14 kpc by radio parallax, one of the most accurate distances to any black hole binary

jets.source: Resolved, rapidly changing radio jets were imaged during the 2015 outburst

objects.name: A0620−00
objects.blurb: The nearest known black hole to Earth, quiet since its 1975 outburst — and one of the few with a spin measured to be genuinely low.

solarMasses.source: Cantrell et al. (2010), ApJ 710, 1127 — 6.61 ± 0.25 M☉ from ~30 years of photometry with the variable disk component removed

spin.source: Gou et al. (2010), ApJL 718, L122 — a* = 0.12 ± 0.19 by continuum fitting (a* < 0.49 at 3σ); a genuinely slowly spinning black hole

jets.source: A compact radio jet is detected even in quiescence despite the low spin — evidence the jet is disk-driven rather than spin-driven — but there is no prominent large-scale jet to render

objects.name: GRO J1655−40
objects.blurb: The second superluminal source found in the galaxy, and the textbook case for measuring spin from the thermal disk continuum.

solarMasses.source: Optical dynamical mass, 5.4 ± 0.3 M☉ (Beer & Podsiadlowski 2002 and subsequent redeterminations)

spin.source: Shafee et al. (2006) find a* = 0.65–0.75 by continuum fitting; X-ray timing analyses have argued for markedly different values, so the intermediate spin is not settled

inclinationDeg.source: 69 ± 2° — a high-inclination system, close to edge-on, which is why its eclipses and dips are so pronounced

distanceKpc.source: ~3.2 kpc is the commonly adopted value; there is no parallax and published estimates range from roughly 1.7 to 3.2 kpc

jets.source: Apparently superluminal radio jets were resolved during the 1994 outburst

objects.name: M87*
objects.blurb: The first black hole ever imaged, in the giant elliptical M87 — and not in the Milky Way. Its jet is visible from Earth in an amateur telescope's reach of the galaxy's core.

solarMasses.source: EHT Collaboration (2019), First M87 EHT Results I & VI — (6.5 ± 0.7)e9 M☉ from the measured shadow diameter

spin.source: EHT modelling requires non-zero spin to power the jet, and a precessing jet nozzle (Cui et al. 2023) implies a spinning hole, but no measurement pins a* — ~0.9 is a frequently quoted claim, not a settled value

inclinationDeg.source: Jet axis inclination ≈ 17° to the line of sight from superluminal motion in the jet — nearly face-on, which is why the shadow appears so circular

jets.source: The M87 jet is one of the most studied relativistic jets in astronomy, resolved from radio to X-ray
